newsitem.title: UK: BA, American launch alliance campaign in US.
newsitem.headline: BA, American launch alliance campaign in US.

text.p: British Airways Plc and American Airlines said on Friday they had submitted a joint application to the U.S. Department of Transportation (DoT) requesting formal approval for their planned alliance.

The move marks the start of the final but what industry analysts and other airlines say could prove the most difficult and longest stage in the two airlines' attempts to win regulatory approvals for their controversial deal.
The U.S. process is tied to Britain and the U.S. negotiating a new "open skies" aviation trade pact at the same time.
But BA's chief executive Robert Ayling said he was still hopeful of completing approvals in time for the original planned start of the alliance in April.

"We had said at the time we announced this (deal) back in the summer last year that we wanted to begin commercial operations from April 1997. We are optimistic," he told Reuters in Bangalore, southern India.
Ayling was accompanying British Prime Minister John Major on a visit to the Indian sub-continent.
Rival airlines have already said they intend to oppose the application in the U.S., arguing that the proposed tie-up will dominate the British transatlantic market with over 60 percent of capacity.

But BA and American say the deal will lead to more competition because it will only go ahead if Britain and the U.S. agree an open skies aviation trade pact allowing all U.S. airlines into London Heathrow, Europe's most popular landfall.

"Our filing today represents a significant milestone towards the launch of our alliance and the introduction of the great benefits it promises for all transatlantic travellers," Ayling said in a statement.
It was confirmed on Thursday that British and U.S. officials are to resume open skies talks in Washington on February 4.

"The governments of the United States and the United Kingdon have each said they want to achieve the open skies agreement that is a prerequisite to approval of our alliance," American's chairman Robert Crandall said on Friday.

Ayling told Reuters in Bangalore: "I think if the British government were able to secure a new bilateral (deal) and terms can be agreed with the regulators this will mark the final and major achievement in a period of policy liberalisation which started with the privatisation of BA (in 1987)...now through to an open skies agreement with the largest aviation market in the world.
"In 1977 (the date of the last Anglo-U.S. aviation services agreement) such a policy would have been unthinkable."
